extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, appellate counsel, judges, and law clerks working on patent infringement and damages disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria used by the Federal Circuit in reviewing district-court rulings on §101 patent eligibility, infringement JMOL, and Rule 59 motions for new trial on damages (reasonable royalty/admissibility of damages expert testimony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step test for §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court’s two-step test: at Alice step one, review whether a claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea); at Alice step two, review whether the claim recites elements sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Alice step one to identify whether the claimed concept is an abstract idea; if so, apply step two to determine whether the claim adds an inventive concept or elements that transform the idea into patent-eligible subject matter. (Cites: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank, 573 U.S. 208.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealability of denial of summary judgment after trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court’s denial of summary judgment is not appealable after a trial on the merits; a denial of summary judgment is not a judgment and only indicates that genuine issues of material fact exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the §101 issue was tried on the merits, the full trial record supersedes the summary-judgment record and the denial of summary judgment is not separately appealable. (Cites: Syngenta, Ortiz, Glaros.)

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 conventionality inquiry (jury question)
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, the jury was asked whether the elements of the asserted claim, individually and as an ordered combination, involved activities or technology that were 'well-understood, routine, or conventional' to a skilled artisan at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The party asserting ineligibility must prove by clear and convincing evidence that claim elements were well-understood, routine, or conventional; factual record (testimony, evidence) can resolve this for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: JMOL review standard and substantial-evidence test
rubrics_metrics.description: JMOL (judgment as a matter of law) motions are reviewed under regional-circuit law; the Fifth Circuit reviews de novo the grant or denial of JMOL, but a jury verdict is upheld if supported by substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On appeal, examine whether there is substantial evidence—i.e., relevant evidence a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support the conclusion—to sustain the jury’s verdict. Consider all evidence presented at trial, including expert testimony and documents. (Cites: Energy Transp. Group; ClearValue; Med. Care Am.; In re Mouttet.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial evidence is 'relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing a jury verdict for sufficiency, defer to the jury so long as such substantial evidence exists (including expert testimony, documentary evidence, source code, web documentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence supporting infringement findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony, documentary evidence (e.g., website guides), and source code can constitute substantial evidence that an accused device meets a claim limitation (e.g., 'receives temperature measurements from inside the structure').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroborating documentary evidence and conceded testimony from opposing experts strengthen an infringement finding; focus on whether evidence supports the claimed functional reading (not just the device’s internal measurements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 59 new-trial standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A new trial may be granted if the verdict is against the weight of the evidence, damages awarded are excessive, the trial was unfair, or prejudicial error was committed; the party seeking a new trial bears the burden of showing harmful error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review of denial of a Rule 59 motion is for abuse of discretion under regional-circuit law. Courts do not grant new trials absent a reasonably clear showing of prejudicial error or substantial injustice. (Cites: Seidman; Jordan; Fornesa.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of damages expert testimony (methodology tied to facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissibility centers on whether the methodology employed by the damages expert is reliable and sufficiently tied to the particular facts of the case; testimony that is speculative or guesswork is inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reliability (Daubert/Kumho/Joiner principles): expert should explain methodology, tie opinions to case facts (licenses, documents, testimony), and avoid leaving the jury to 'fill in the gaps.' (Cites: Summit, Virnetx, Whitserve, Wordtech.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical negotiation approach for reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothetical negotiation (Georgia-Pacific style) 'necessarily involves an element of approximation and uncertainty' and attempts to determine what the parties would have agreed to as a royalty at the time of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts may use comparable licenses, business documents, testimony, and economic data to estimate a reasonable royalty; the methodology must be fact-based and defensible, and the jury can weigh approximation vs. precision. (Cites: Lucent; Mueller on Patent Enforcement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving per-unit royalty from lump-sum licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on lump-sum (portfolio or settlement) licenses, an expert must show how the lump-sum amounts were calculated or otherwise convert them to a per-unit royalty—licenses that merely recite a per-unit 'belief' without calculation are weak support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'plucking' a per-unit rate from recitals; provide documents or testimony showing the parties actually applied the per-unit rate or a defensible conversion. Cases caution against using lump-sum licenses without evidence of the calculation (Wordtech, Whitserve, MLC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparability and built-in apportionment of licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A comparable license is sufficiently comparable when principles of apportionment are effectively 'baked into' the license—i.e., the royalty rate and base reflect the value of the asserted patent relative to other package elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a license is economically and technically comparable, it may carry built-in apportionment so further apportionment is unnecessary. Experts should account for differences in technology and economic circumstances between past licenses and the hypothetical negotiation. (Cites: Omega; Finjan; ActiveVideo; Bio-Rad.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment to the patented improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages must reflect the value of only the patented improvement; the patentee must give evidence tending to 'separate or apportion' the value of the patented feature from unpatented features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts must either use sufficiently comparable licenses that embody apportionment or separately apportion using record evidence (e.g., feature-level profit attribution, surveys). Failure to tie the royalty to the specific patent can render the opinion unreliable. (Cites: Omega; Virnetx; Apple.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court gatekeeping vs. jury's credibility/weighing role
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court must act as gatekeeper to screen expert methodology for reliability, but credibility determinations, weighing of evidence, and drawing inferences are for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not elevate admissibility into wholesale exclusion where methodology is sound and tied to facts; conversely, do not abdicate the gatekeeper role—ensure experts address the right factual questions so the jury can evaluate subjective matters. (Cites: Joiner; Kumho; Reeves.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of internal profit and survey data for apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert may ground apportionment on internal profit figures and customer survey data to estimate the percentage of profits attributable to the patented technology and thereby justify a royalty rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such internal data can provide an independent cross-check of a proposed royalty rate, but the methodology must not be circularly premised on the same contested royalty figure being tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual disputes on comparability resolved by cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of comparability of licenses and other factual disputes about economic circumstances are generally factual issues to be addressed by cross-examination and jury determination, not automatic exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the expert’s methodology is sound and the evidence sufficiently related to the case, permit testimony and let opposing counsel probe weaknesses at trial. (Cites: ActiveVideo; Bio-Rad.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-serving recitals and unsupported assertions are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A party’s unilateral licensor 'recitals' stating a 'belief' about a per-unit royalty (or other self-serving statements) are weak support absent corroborating calculations, sales data, or contrary contractual language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for license language that expressly states a lump sum 'is not based upon sales and does not reflect or constitute a royalty'—such disclaimers undercut reliance on recital-based royalty conversions. Experts should supply independent evidence of how lump sums relate to per-unit rates. (Discussed in dissent; cites Wordtech/MLC/Whitserve.)
